channel.title: The Pointe at Kirby Gate: Senior Living News
channel.description: Senior housing, senior care and caregiving news from trusted publishers, gathered every day by our team. The summaries are ours; the full stories belong to their publishers.

item.title: Report: staffing now takes about 48% of senior living revenue as residents need more care
item.description: Senior Housing News covers a new industry report that looks at why demand for senior living is strong while construction of new communities is not. One finding concerns staffing: it took an average of 48% of revenue in 2025, compared with 39% ten years earlier. The authors say the main driver is probably that residents now arrive needing more care than in the past, more than the extra staff required as buildings fill up. Why it matters: Few new communities and higher care needs can mean fewer openings, which is a reason for families to start looking early.

item.title: Researcher says dementia diagnosis is not keeping pace with new treatments as care needs grow
item.description: An Alzheimer's researcher at the University of Kansas told Senior Housing News that the system for diagnosing dementia has fallen behind the newer treatments now available. He pointed to memory clinic waitlists that can run for months and a shortage of dementia specialists as the main barriers. The article notes that 44% of assisted living residents live with Alzheimer's or another form of dementia, which makes earlier and faster diagnosis a growing concern for families and the communities that care for them. Why it matters: An earlier diagnosis gives a family more time to plan care and choose the right setting before a crisis.

item.title: Blood-test markers help estimate who may develop memory problems within 5 to 10 years, study finds
item.description: A study in JAMA Neurology looked at older adults who had no memory or thinking problems but whose tests showed Alzheimer's-related changes in the brain. Using long-running research groups, including the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging, researchers estimated each person's chance of developing mild cognitive impairment or dementia over 5 and 10 years. Higher starting levels of a blood marker called p-tau217 were tied to a greater risk, and risk also rose with age. The goal is clearer, personal risk estimates instead of a simple yes-or-no result. Families with questions about memory testing should talk to their doctor. Why it matters: Blood tests are entering memory checkups, so families may hear about these markers at a parent's next visit.

item.title: Social Security is notifying some Medicare enrollees who must confirm eligibility under new immigration-status rules
item.description: The Social Security Administration says a federal law enacted in July 2025 narrows who can be entitled to Medicare. Eligibility is now limited to U.S. citizens and nationals, lawful permanent residents and a few other specific immigration categories. SSA is mailing letters this month to current enrollees whose eligibility it cannot confirm or who no longer qualify, and it says Medicare coverage may end on February 1, 2027 for people whose eligibility is not confirmed. The agency notes the change does not affect eligibility for Social Security benefits or how they are paid. CMS actuaries estimate about 32,000 people will lose coverage. Why it matters: Families who help an older relative with mail should watch for these letters, since SSA says unconfirmed eligibility can end Medicare coverage on February 1.

item.title: New guide: choosing assisted living near East Memphis and Germantown
item.description: Our new guide is for families comparing assisted living close to home in East Memphis, Germantown and Collierville. It suggests starting with the relative who will visit most, driving the route at a real visiting hour, and keeping a parent's doctors, pharmacy and weekly routines within reach. It explains how Tennessee licenses assisted care living facilities, how to ask a community for its latest state survey, and how the Long-Term Care Ombudsman can help. It also covers what to look for when a parent has memory loss and ends with a checklist for comparing nearby communities. Why it matters: Distance narrows the list, but level of care, inspection history and a parent's routines decide the right fit.

item.title: Study links high-dose flu shots to lower Alzheimer's risk in adults 65 and older
item.description: Researchers at UTHealth Houston, publishing in the journal Neurology, compared older adults who received a high-dose flu vaccine with those who received the standard dose. In this large records-based study, the high-dose group was less likely to be diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease in the years that followed, and the link appeared stronger in women. Because the study was observational, it shows an association, not proof that the vaccine prevents Alzheimer's, and the authors call for further research. Why it matters: Flu season is here; families with an older parent can ask their doctor which flu vaccine is right for them.

item.title: New Congress expected to look harder at senior living ownership, staffing and affordability
item.description: Senior Housing News reports that the incoming Congress is likely to give senior living more attention. Lawmakers have signaled interest in how communities are owned and financed, including private equity and real estate investment structures, and in staffing and workforce practices. At the same time, industry groups see openings to work on affordability for middle-income older adults. Assisted living is regulated mainly by the states, and the industry's trade group says it plans to explain to lawmakers how assisted living differs from nursing homes. Why it matters: Families comparing communities can expect more public attention on who owns a community and how it is staffed, both good questions to ask on any tour.

item.title: CDC: nearly half of assisted living communities care for residents with dementia, heart disease, diabetes and depression
item.description: A new data brief from the CDC's National Center for Health Statistics, drawn from its 2025 national survey of residential care communities (the federal category that includes assisted living), found that 48% of communities had current residents living with each of four common chronic conditions: Alzheimer's disease or another dementia, heart disease, diabetes and depression. About 19% more reported three of the four. Communities with 11 or more beds, those outside metro areas and those in the Northeast and Midwest were more likely to report all four. Communities that did were also more likely to report resident emergency department visits, overnight hospital stays and falls. Why it matters: Many assisted living residents live with several chronic conditions at once, so it helps to ask any community how it supports dementia, diabetes, heart and mood-related care needs.

item.title: Medicare finalizes 2027 home health payment rule with a 2.4% increase and new anti-fraud checks
item.description: The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services has finalized its 2027 payment rule for Medicare home health agencies, the providers that send nurses and therapists to the homes of eligible, homebound beneficiaries. According to Home Health Care News, the rule raises payments by 2.4%, the same increase as in 2026 and about $415 million more overall. It also adds several fraud-prevention measures, most of which apply to every type of Medicare-enrolled provider, and recognizes home health's role in palliative care, with examples to follow in later guidance. CMS did not finalize a new home health wage index method. The provisions take effect January 1, 2027. Why it matters: Medicare home health is often part of a hospital discharge plan for an older adult, and this rule shapes how those agencies are paid and screened starting in January.

item.title: AARP report: caregiving can cost working family caregivers about $120,500 in lifetime income
item.description: A new AARP report released November 4, "The Hidden Cost of Caregiving," estimates how cutting back on paid work to care for a relative affects a family caregiver's finances over a lifetime. Using an Urban Institute economic model, researchers put the average loss for a working caregiver at about $120,500 in today's dollars, mostly in lost wages, with the rest in reduced workplace retirement income and smaller Social Security benefits. The estimates are modeled for caregivers born in the early 1980s. Caregivers who give up more than 5,000 work hours face far larger losses, very few working caregivers in the analysis kept their full hours, and AARP puts the national total at roughly $2.3 trillion. Why it matters: Adult children balancing a job and a parent's care often feel the cost years later; this report puts numbers on that tradeoff and can help start family conversations about sharing the load.

item.title: Stanford study: resting brain activity may signal Alzheimer's risk years before memory problems
item.description: Stanford Medicine researchers compared brain scans taken at rest from 180 older adults whose memory has stayed exceptionally sharp, often called super agers, and 110 people with Alzheimer's disease. From the differences, they built a score that told the two groups apart about 85% of the time. When the score was applied to more than 1,300 adults aged 55 to 70 with no thinking problems, people whose brain activity looked more like the Alzheimer's group were more likely to show later decline and an Alzheimer's diagnosis. The study appears in Science Advances. The researchers say the method is not ready for use in a doctor's office and that one score does not decide anyone's future. Why it matters: Research like this may one day help doctors spot risk earlier; families with memory concerns should talk to their doctor.

item.title: NPR: The cost of caring for an aging relative is climbing, and Medicare covers little of it
item.description: In an NPR conversation, a journalist who covers aging explains why the cost of caring for an older relative so often catches families by surprise. Drawing on recent AARP research showing that family caregivers now spend roughly 60% more of their own money than they did five years ago, the segment notes that Medicare pays for very little long-term care. Apart from short stays after a hospitalization, it does not cover everyday help with bathing, dressing or meals. The discussion also points out that typical retirement savings fall well short of what years of paid care can add up to. Why it matters: Knowing early what Medicare will and won't pay for gives families time to plan; a benefits counselor or elder law attorney can help sort out the options.

item.title: Alzheimer's Association honors nearly 13 million dementia caregivers during Family Caregivers Month
item.description: For National Family Caregivers Month, the Alzheimer's Association is recognizing the nearly 13 million Americans who give unpaid care to someone living with Alzheimer's or another dementia, under the 2026 theme "Caregiving Changes Everything." The Association notes that a diagnosis reshapes daily life for the whole family, and it is sharing stories from spouses, adult children, grandchildren and friends throughout November. It also points caregivers to its free resources, including a 24/7 Helpline, support groups, care planning tools, education programs and a monthly on-demand webinar series. Anyone can send a note of thanks to a caregiver through the Association's Honor a Caregiver campaign. Why it matters: Caring for someone with dementia is a long road, and free, around-the-clock support is available so no family has to manage it alone.

item.title: What Is Respite Care and When Should You Use It?
item.description: Our new guide explains respite care: short-term care for an older adult so the usual family caregiver can rest, travel or recover. It describes the main forms, from in-home help and adult day programs to short residential stays, and lists warning signs that a caregiver needs a break, such as constant exhaustion and putting off their own health care. It also covers what to look for when a parent has dementia, where Memphis families can find caregiver support, and a checklist for planning a stay that goes smoothly. Why it matters: Planning a break before burnout sets in helps family caregivers keep caring for a parent over the long run.

item.title: Minnesota's assisted living report card shows how residents and families judge quality
item.description: McKnight's Senior Living reports on an industry session that reviewed how Minnesota and Oregon are working to measure assisted living quality. Minnesota's Assisted Living Report Card, modeled on the state's nursing home report card, rates licensed communities using resident quality-of-life and family satisfaction surveys along with state inspection findings on safety and staffing. People consulted in building the tool ranked quality of life, staff quality and resident safety as the most important areas. In the survey results, family members were less satisfied overall than residents, and food was the lowest-rated area for both groups. Why it matters: Quality of life, staffing, safety and food are worth asking about on any assisted living tour, in Tennessee or anywhere else.

item.title: Does Medicare Pay for Assisted Living? What It Covers
item.description: Our new guide answers a question many families ask during Medicare open enrollment. Medicare does not pay for assisted living, because room, meals and daily personal care are not covered. The guide explains what Medicare still covers when a parent lives in assisted living: doctors, hospital care and prescriptions, part-time home health services, hospice, and short-term skilled nursing rehab after a qualifying hospital stay of at least three days. It also lists questions to ask before the December 7 enrollment deadline and points families to Tennessee's free, unbiased SHIP Medicare counseling. Why it matters: Knowing what Medicare does and does not cover helps families plan before a hospital discharge forces a decision.

item.title: Assisted Living vs. Memory Care: What's the Difference?
item.description: Our new guide compares assisted living and memory care, two settings that are easy to confuse. It explains how they differ in who they serve, safety and secured spaces, dementia training for staff, and how daily life is structured. It notes that in Tennessee, assisted living is licensed by the state's Health Facilities Commission and is not a nursing home. The guide also lists signs that a parent with memory loss may need memory care, and questions worth bringing on a tour. Why it matters: Choosing the right setting from the start can spare a parent a second move later.

item.title: Alzheimer's Association: planning holiday gatherings around a loved one with dementia
item.description: With Thanksgiving approaching, the Alzheimer's Association's holiday guidance suggests planning ahead and keeping celebrations simple when a family member is living with dementia. Ideas include talking with relatives beforehand about changes in memory and behavior, holding the meal earlier in the day for people who tend to become confused or restless in the evening, and inviting the person to help with familiar, manageable tasks such as setting the table. The Association notes that smaller gatherings may work better, that no caregiver has to keep every tradition, and that relatives can help by giving the primary caregiver even an hour of relief. Why it matters: A little planning can make Thanksgiving calmer for a parent with dementia and less exhausting for the family caregiver.

item.title: Survey: families use AI to build senior living shortlists, but tours and staff still decide
item.description: A U.S. News & World Report survey of 502 U.S. adults who were researching senior living, or had recently moved a relative or themselves into a community, found that about 70% used generative AI tools during the search, most often to compare communities on a shortlist. About half of those able to judge said they had run into wrong AI-generated information, most often about the level of care or amenities a community offers and about availability or wait times. Final decisions still hinged on in-person tours and conversations with staff and residents, and three in four respondents said they would check an independent source before choosing. Why it matters: AI tools can speed up a search, but care levels and availability are worth confirming directly with each community, in person.

item.title: Flu season 2026-2027: what the National Council on Aging says older adults should know
item.description: The National Council on Aging has updated its flu season guide for 2026-2027. NCOA reports that in a September 1 update the CDC kept its earlier seasonal flu vaccine recommendations in place, including a preference for certain enhanced vaccines for people 65 and older. The guide notes that in August 2026 the FDA approved the first mRNA flu vaccine in the U.S. for adults 50 and older. NCOA adds that a flu shot can still be given later in the season, that the vaccine lowers the risk of severe illness even if it does not prevent every case, and when to seek care after getting sick. Why it matters: With flu season starting and family gatherings ahead, it is a good time to talk to your doctor, or a parent's doctor, about which vaccines fit.
